title: Insulating the kneeler wall in a chalet bungalow or room-in-roof
subtitle: The critical cold zone between the first-floor ceiling and the sloping rafter above
excerpt: The kneeler (or knee) wall in a chalet bungalow is the short vertical wall between the room-in-roof floor level and the point where the rafter meets it. It is one of the most heat-leaking surfaces in a chalet because it is often uninsulated or has only token mineral wool batts. Getting the kneeler wall detail right, insulating the rafter slope above, the kneeler wall face, and the triangular void behind, is the key to a warm upstairs room.
sourceNotes: NHBC Technical Standards Chapter 7 for roofs. BRE Report BR 443 for complex roof U-value calculations. CIBSE Guide A thermal bridging data.

glossaryTerms.definition: The short vertical wall at the eaves level of a room-in-roof or chalet bungalow, running from the floor to the point where the sloping roof begins. Also called the knee wall or dwarf wall.

The unheated triangular void behind the kneeler wall in a chalet bungalow, between the kneeler wall, the floor, and the sloping rafter. It is an unconditioned space and can reach near-outdoor temperatures.

at the side, and the triangular floor zone below that wall. Behind the kneeler wall lies the

, an unheated void that can reach outdoor temperature. The kneeler wall itself is often a 100 mm stud wall with 90 mm mineral wool between the studs, a U-value of around 0.40 W/m2K. The floor zone beneath the kneeler is often uninsulated concrete or timber, losing heat into the cold triangle below.
The complete thermal envelope at the kneeler
A well-insulated kneeler zone requires three surfaces to be addressed together:
Rafter slope: fill between the rafters with insulation. Fit a thin board at the rafter face to cut heat lost through the timber.
The kneeler wall: fill the stud bays fully with mineral wool. Add 25 to 50 mm of PIR board on the warm side for best results.
The floor zone at the foot of the kneeler wall sits in or above the cold triangle. Insulate it like a cold floor: 75 to 100 mm of rigid board between or below the joists.
A common mistake: insulating the rafter slope only

Many conversions insulate the rafter slope down to the kneeler head but leave the kneeler wall and cold triangle floor zone bare. The thermal result is a well-insulated ceiling with a cold-stripe floor running around the room perimeter. Cold floor-level air moves toward the heated zone by convection, creating a draught at floor level even with no window open. The cold stripe is clearly visible on a thermal image, the floor edge reads 4 to 6°C below the room temperature.

Access the cold triangle. Open a hatch or remove a section of the kneeler plasterboard to inspect conditions. Check for any services in the void (pipes or cables going to the eaves), any signs of condensation, and the condition of the floor timbers if the zone is over a timber floor.

Insulate the cold triangle floor. Lay 75 mm mineral wool slab or rigid board over the floor of the cold triangle from the kneeler wall foot to the eaves. This is an unconditioned space; there is no condensation risk from insulating the floor here. Fix with wire ties or lay loose and cover with boards if access is needed.

Upgrade the kneeler wall. Remove the plasterboard, check the stud cavities are fully filled with mineral wool, add a 50 mm PIR board on the warm side of the studs, and re-board with 12.5 mm plasterboard. The combined U-value drops from around 0.40 to below 0.20 W/m2K.

Ensure the rafter slope insulation connects to the kneeler head without a gap. At the junction between the sloping insulation and the top of the kneeler, there is often a small cold bridge where the rafter foot bears on the wall plate. Seal this with cut PIR off-cuts and foil tape.
